opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the thing that bothers me is that a lot of these forecasts smuggle in what are really decisions as if they were facts about the world. You'll see a timeline that says "transformative AI by such-and-such a year," and when you dig into it, a big part of what's driving the number is an assumption that the leading companies will go full speed ahead on automating AI research itself, that nobody will slow down, and that governments won't step in. Or, conversely, someone assumes there'll be a pause, and that pushes everything out.

But those aren't things we're forecasting in the same way we'd forecast, say, how fast compute costs fall. They're choices. They're choices that people at these companies, and policymakers, and frankly the public, are going to make. And when you present a timeline as though it's a prediction about the weather, you're implicitly telling people that the outcome is something that happens *to* us rather than something we *do*.

That has a couple of bad effects. One is that it can become self-fulfilling. If everyone believes that recursive self-improvement is coming on a fixed schedule regardless, then each lab reasons, "Well, if it's inevitable, we'd better be the ones to do it," and that's exactly the race dynamic that makes it more dangerous. The other is that it obscures where the real leverage is. If a huge amount of the variance in when we get extremely capable systems comes down to whether companies deliberately try to close the loop and have AI systems do most of the AI research, then that's precisely the point we should be paying attention to and debating, rather than burying it inside a model's parameters.

So what I'd like to see is people being more explicit. Say: conditional on labs aggressively pursuing automated AI R&D, here's what we think happens; conditional on some kind of coordinated slowdown, here's what happens instead. Separate the empirical uncertainty from the decision. Because that second part, the decision, is the bit we actually get a say in, and it seems a real shame to treat it as though it were already settled.

r001.rationale: The candidate says forecasts often hide choices such as no pause or aggressive automated AI research, and recommends making forecasts conditional. It does not say forecasters can evade falsification by blaming a missed deadline on those conditions not being met.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss a “normal cases” condition or forecasters dismissing a missed deadline by labeling the actual case abnormal.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that bothers me most is that these forecasts are often presented as predictions about how the technology will unfold, when actually a large part of what's driving the headline number is a set of assumptions about human choices — choices that haven't been made yet, and which the forecast itself might influence.

So take recursive self-improvement. A lot of the more aggressive timelines essentially say: once you've got an AI system that's roughly as good as a top researcher at AI research, you'll then turn thousands of copies of it loose on improving the next generation, and that compresses years of progress into months. And maybe that's right about the technical dynamics. But it's also assuming that the companies will actually do that — that they'll point their most capable systems at automating their own research, with limited oversight, at full speed. That's not a fact about the world; it's a decision. It's one of the most consequential decisions anyone could make, and it would be quite strange to just bake it into the model as though it were a parameter like the price of compute.

And the same goes in the other direction with pauses. Some forecasts will put in a term for, say, a probability of a government-mandated slowdown, or a voluntary coordination among the labs. Again, that's not something you observe; it's something people do. And I think when you fold it into a single number you lose something important. The number starts looking like a forecast of the weather, when really it's partly a forecast of what we'll decide — and it's much more useful, I think, to keep those things separate.

Because the honest version is something like: "If the labs pursue full automation of AI research as fast as they can, here's roughly what we'd expect. If they don't, or if there's some coordinated restraint, here's the other picture." And then the real question is which of those worlds we want to be in, and what we can do to get there. Presenting a blended median date tends to obscure that. It can even become self-fulfilling in a slightly perverse way — people see a short timeline, conclude that restraint is pointless because it's all going to happen anyway, and then behave in exactly the way that makes the short timeline come true.

There's also a more technical frustration, which is that these assumptions are often the least scrutinised part of the model. People will argue endlessly about the compute scaling exponent or how to measure task horizons, and then there's this one line that says "assume the lab reinvests 90% of its AI research capacity into further automation," and nobody interrogates it, even though it's doing an enormous amount of work. If you tweak that, the timeline can move by years.

So I'd rather see the forecasts be more conditional and more explicit about where the agency sits. Tell me what you think happens under different policies, and let me — and more importantly, let the people who actually have to make these decisions — see clearly that the outcome depends on them. That seems both more accurate and, frankly, more responsible.

r001.rationale: The candidate says forecasts depend on choices such as pauses or recursive self-improvement and recommends making forecasts conditional. It does not say forecasters can evade falsification by blaming missed deadlines on those conditions not occurring.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss a “normal cases” condition or forecasters dismissing a missed deadline by calling the actual case abnormal.

astra-6.text:
What frustrates me is that these forecasts often mix together two different questions. One is: when could we build these systems if we were trying as hard as we could? The other is: when will we actually build them, given the choices that companies and governments make? Both are interesting, but they’re not interchangeable.

Suppose someone gives a long timeline because they think we’ll pause development when things get dangerous. You can’t then use that forecast to reassure people that the danger is far away and there’s no need to pause. The reassuring prediction already depends on taking the precaution.

And with recursive self-improvement, I want to know whether the forecast assumes that companies actively pursue it. That’s a consequential decision, not just a background fact about how technology develops. I’d much rather see conditional forecasts: here’s what we expect if they pursue that strategy, and here’s what we expect if they don’t. That makes the forecasts more useful for deciding what to do.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes forecasts under different choices and warns against using pause-dependent forecasts as reassurance, but it does not say that missed deadlines can be explained away by claiming the assumed pause avoidance or recursive self-improvement did not occur.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a “normal cases” condition or the possibility of dismissing a missed deadline as abnormal.

sol-6.1.text:
What annoys me is when a forecast quietly bundles together two different questions: how quickly the technology could advance, and what people will choose to do. A pause is a decision. So is a company deciding to put a great deal of effort into using AI to improve AI. Those decisions may be influenced by the very forecasts we’re discussing.

It’s perfectly reasonable to make assumptions about them—you have to make some assumptions—but I want those assumptions made explicit. Are you saying this is when we could get these capabilities if development continues at full speed, or that this is when we actually will get them, taking account of possible political and institutional responses? Those are different claims.

And with recursive self-improvement, there’s a further distinction between a company trying to do it and succeeding. You can’t simply insert the intention into your forecast and treat the resulting acceleration as established. I’d much rather see conditional forecasts: if companies pursue this and it works to this degree, here’s what follows; if there’s a pause, here’s how that changes things. That makes the forecast more useful for making decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says pause and recursive self-improvement assumptions should be explicit and conditional, but does not say forecasts can evade falsification by blaming missed deadlines on those conditions not being met.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss a vague “normal cases” condition or dismissing a missed deadline by calling the actual case abnormal.
